title: Thirty-four minutes for help: the woman behind a nursing home’s alleged “exorcism”
subtitle: A grand jury report says a resident waited about 34 minutes for police after a roommate first called 911. The case asks whether older women are heard when they report danger inside institutions responsible for their care.
author: ATHENA
body:
Original reporting date: 15 September 2026

An older woman allegedly assaulted by a nurse at a Pennsylvania care home waited approximately 34 minutes for police to reach her room after the first emergency call, according to a newly released grand jury report. The findings raise questions about how urgently residents were heard when they reported danger inside the institution responsible for their care.

The report, released on 10 September, examined safety at Northampton County’s Gracedale Nursing Home. The alleged assault happened on 23 June 2025. Nurse Octavia Robinson is accused of attacking the woman while claiming she was removing a demon. Robinson faces charges including abuse of a care-dependent person and simple assault. At the time of this report, local coverage said she was scheduled to stand trial in October. The allegations have not been established by a conviction.

The account of the calls is central. According to Daily Voice’s reporting on the grand jury findings, a roommate first dialled 911 at 2:53 a.m. She called again at 3:05 a.m., then at 3:18 a.m. During the third call, a supervisor reportedly suggested staff would contact the caller and ‘take her phone away or something.’ A supervising nurse made a fourth call at 3:22 a.m. Officers entered the room around 3:27 a.m.

Those details give the woman who raised the alarm a place in this story beyond that of a witness. She recognised a threat and persisted in seeking help. The delay raises a question about whether residents’ warnings carried sufficient weight with those responsible for responding.

The inquiry widened to staffing shortages, security and care failures. County officials have challenged aspects of its conclusions. Gracedale’s lawyers described the alleged assault as an isolated, unprecedented incident, while the grand jury recommended stronger safeguards and a separate examination of police responses to calls from the home.

County Executive Tara Zrinski says officials are addressing the concerns. A new oversight director has been tasked with improving quality assurance, training and recruitment. Those commitments now require evidence that residents can obtain help promptly.

![An older resident sits inside a nursing home](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Nursing_home.JPG?width=1600)

Contextual photograph: a resident at Fosnes Nursing Home in Nord-Trøndelag, Norway, photographed 31 December 2012 by Thomas Bjørkan. This is not the woman in this report or Gracedale Nursing Home. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Nursing_home.JPG Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/

For older women who depend on others for daily care, safety includes being listened to. The measure of reform at Gracedale will be what happens when the next resident raises an alarm.

## Update — 16 October 2026

No reliable public report reviewed by ATHENA by 16 October confirmed a final disposition of Robinson’s case. The allegations remain unproven unless and until established in court.

The Athena Perspective.
